Eleven days. Every plan we built assumed three hundred.
First problem. The grid. When the flare hits, every power line becomes an antenna, and whatever is plugged into one gets cooked.
Day two. We cut the house off the grid completely. A manual transfer switch, nine hundred dollars. From here on, we run on our own panels or we run on nothing.
Day four. Every spare electronic goes into a Faraday cage. A steel bin, lined with cardboard, lid sealed with copper tape. Radio, laptop, spare charge controller, inside.
Day six. The panels themselves are fine. It is the long wiring runs that pick up the surge, so we fit surge arrestors at both ends. Fourteen hundred dollars.
Day eight. We fill everything that holds water. Both tanks, the bath, forty jerry cans. The pumps might survive. They might not.
Day ten. Last run to town. The shelves are already stripped. We buy nothing, and we drive home.
Day eleven. Four twelve in the morning, the sky turns green.
The transformer on our road exploded. Every house in the valley went dark in the same second.
Ours did not. The fridge hummed. The tap ran. And the radio, in its steel bin, still worked.
One point six million dollars, two hundred and twenty days, and ten episodes of being called paranoid.
That is the Solar Flash series. Which build would you have done first?
